cards.title: The ML Lifecycle at a Glance
cards.teaser: Machine learning is not a one-shot activity — it is a loop. Data feeds training, training produces a model, evaluation validates it, deployment serves it, monitoring watches it, and retraining renews it. Understanding the full loop is the prerequisite for operating it reliably.

runs.text: The ML lifecycle is most clearly seen as a closed loop with six major stages:

Each stage is a forcing function for the next. Bad data produces bad models. A model that passes offline evaluation may still drift in production. A model that has drifted is the trigger for retraining. The loop is the unit of delivery in ML, not the single experiment.

This structure differs fundamentally from a software delivery lifecycle. In software, the artifact — compiled code — does not degrade on its own. In ML, the model is a function of the data distribution it was trained on, and that distribution is always changing. The loop is not optional engineering overhead; it is the mechanism by which the model stays correct.

Google's MLOps whitepaper ("MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning," cloud.google.com/architecture/mlops-continuous-delivery-and-automation-pipelines-in-machine-learning) frames the entire MLOps discipline around automating this loop to different degrees — what it calls maturity levels 0, 1, and 2.
The ML lifecycle is a loop, not a line: collect data, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor, retrain — then repeat. The loop never stops because the world keeps changing and the model must keep up.

cards.title: How the ML Lifecycle Differs from Software Lifecycles
cards.teaser: Software is built once and deployed; ML models are built repeatedly and replaced. Code that passes tests stays correct until changed; a model that passes offline evaluation can degrade in production without a single line of code changing. This distinction drives every MLOps design decision.

runs.text: The software development lifecycle — plan, develop, test, release, operate — treats the artifact as stable until intentionally modified. A compiled binary that passes its test suite today will pass the same test suite in six months unless the code or tests change. Correctness is preserved by version control.
ML upends this assumption in three ways:

items.text: Data dependency.

A model's correctness depends on the statistical relationship between training data and production data. When that relationship changes — user behavior shifts, a new product launches, seasonality kicks in — the model degrades even if no one touched the code or the weights.
Three versioned artifacts, not one.
Software ships one artifact: code. ML ships three: code (training pipeline), data, and model weights. All three must be versioned and reproduced together to get a reproducible result.
Non-deterministic failure.

Software failures are typically discrete: the test passes or it does not. Model degradation is continuous and probabilistic — accuracy drops from 94% to 87% over weeks, which looks like noise until it becomes a business problem.

runs.text: These differences mean that ML teams cannot simply adopt a CI/CD pipeline designed for software and call it done. They need a lifecycle that explicitly governs data, model evaluation, and live performance monitoring — not just build and test.
A software binary stays correct until someone changes the code. A model can become wrong on its own because the world it was trained on has drifted away from the world it is being asked to predict.

cards.title: Data Collection and Labeling
cards.teaser: Labeling is the most underestimated phase in the ML lifecycle — it is slow, expensive, error-prone, and the direct determinant of model quality. Teams that rush labeling spend the rest of the lifecycle debugging symptoms that trace back to noisy ground truth.

runs.text: Data collection and labeling sits at the top of the lifecycle loop but frequently receives the least engineering investment. The common mental model is: "get data → hand it to the data scientist." The operational reality is more demanding.
The labeling problem has several dimensions:

items.text: Scale.
Production models often require millions of labeled examples. Human annotation at that scale requires coordinated workforce management, clear labeling guidelines, and quality audits.
Labeler disagreement.

For subjective tasks — sentiment classification, content moderation, medical imaging — different annotators disagree. Inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa) must be measured and thresholded before labels are accepted.
Label freshness.
Labels defined for last year's product may not reflect this year's use case. A "spam" label defined when email was the channel does not automatically transfer to push notifications.
Feedback label latency.
For some tasks — click prediction, churn prevention — the label is not known until hours or days after the prediction. This creates a labeling pipeline distinct from the batch annotation pipeline.

runs.text: Approaches to reduce labeling cost include weak supervision (Snorkel), active learning (sample the most uncertain predictions for human review), and semi-supervised learning. Each trades annotation fidelity for scale and must be matched to the task's error tolerance.

Andrew Ng's "data-centric AI" framing makes the labeling investment explicit: for many production tasks, improving label quality on 5% of ambiguous examples outperforms adding 50% more raw data. Labeling is not infrastructure — it is model quality work.
Labeling is the phase where humans tell the model what "correct" looks like. Noisy labels mean noisy models, and no training algorithm can fix ground truth that is wrong.

cards.title: Data Validation
cards.teaser: A model trained on clean data will misbehave on dirty production data. Data validation — checking schemas, statistical distributions, and anomalies before training — is the quality gate that prevents garbage-in/garbage-out at scale.

runs.text: Data validation is the discipline of asserting properties about a dataset before it enters training. It occupies the same role in ML that unit tests occupy in software: a fast, automated check that catches known failure modes before they propagate downstream.
Two categories of checks are standard:

items.text: Schema checks.

Expected columns are present and correctly typed. Cardinality of categorical features is within known bounds. No required field is entirely null. These checks catch upstream pipeline breakage — a feature store that stopped writing a column, a schema migration that renamed a field.
Distribution checks.

The statistical properties of each feature match the reference distribution (typically computed from a recent validated training set). Mean, standard deviation, min/max, and histogram shape are all candidates. Large deviations indicate data drift before training begins.

runs.text: Two tools have become reference implementations for this pattern:

items.text: TensorFlow Data Validation (TFDV)

— part of the TFX ecosystem. Computes statistics over a dataset, infers a schema, and validates new datasets against it. Generates alerts on anomalies such as missing features, unexpected values, or distribution shift.
Great Expectations
— a framework-agnostic library that expresses data quality rules as "expectations" (e.g.,
expect_column_values_to_be_between
) and generates data docs (HTML reports) showing pass/fail per expectation.

runs.text: Data validation failures should block the training pipeline — they are the equivalent of a failing CI test. A model trained on anomalous data will produce anomalous predictions, and those predictions will be much harder to debug after deployment.

The pattern: compute a reference schema and statistics from a known-good dataset (the "baseline"), then validate every new training dataset against it. When distribution drift is detected, investigate before training — not after the model underperforms in production.
Data validation is the automated check that asks: "does this data look the way we expect it to look?" If the answer is no, stop and investigate before wasting a training run on bad inputs.

cards.title: Training — The Experiment
cards.teaser: A single training run is an experiment: a specific combination of data, features, hyperparameters, and code produces a model with measured performance. The discipline is making experiments reproducible, tracked, and comparable — not just running them.

runs.text: Training is the stage most people picture when they think of machine learning — fitting a model to data. In a production context, the engineering challenges around training matter as much as the algorithm choices.
A training run has four inputs that must all be versioned to make the run reproducible:

items.text: Training code
— the model architecture, feature engineering pipeline, and training loop. Versioned in git.
Data
— the specific dataset snapshot used for training. Versioned by dataset version or snapshot hash in a data versioning tool (DVC, Delta Lake, ML feature stores).
Hyperparameters
— learning rate, batch size, regularization coefficients, architecture decisions. Logged alongside the run.
Environment
— Python version, framework version, CUDA version. Pinned in a container image or requirements lock file.

runs.text: Experiment tracking tools — MLflow, Weights & Biases, Neptune — exist to log these four inputs alongside the output metrics for every run. Without tracking, teams accumulate "notebook archaeology": searching through dated Jupyter notebooks to reconstruct what was tried and what worked.

At Level 0 in Google's maturity model, training is a manual, script-driven process. A data scientist runs a notebook or script on their local machine or a cloud VM. The resulting model weights are uploaded manually. No version linking, no lineage. This is the industry's most common training setup — and also why many ML projects cannot reproduce their own best model six months later.

Training is an experiment. For it to be useful, you must record what went in — data version, code version, hyperparameters, environment — alongside what came out (metrics), so the experiment is repeatable and comparable to other runs.

cards.title: Evaluation — Offline Metrics and the Metric-Target Gap
cards.teaser: A model that achieves 95% accuracy on a holdout set may still be wrong for production. Offline evaluation measures performance on historical data; online performance is what users experience. The gap between them is where most ML production failures originate.

runs.text: Evaluation is the stage that answers: "is this model good enough to deploy?" It runs on data the model has not seen during training — the holdout or test set.
Standard offline metrics, matched to task type:

items.text: Classification:
accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR. The right metric depends on class imbalance and the cost asymmetry between false positives and false negatives.
Regression:
RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R-squared. RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily; MAE is more robust to outliers.
Ranking / recommendation:
NDCG, MRR, precision@k. Offline ranking metrics correlate imperfectly with online engagement — A/B tests remain the only reliable signal for ranking quality.
Language models:
perplexity, BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore. Automatic metrics for generation correlate loosely with human judgment — human eval is often required for safety-critical use cases.

runs.text: The metric-target gap has two main causes. First, the holdout set is drawn from the same historical distribution as the training data. If production data drifts from that distribution, offline metrics overstate real performance. Second, the metric being optimized may not perfectly proxy business value — a model with higher AUC may produce worse user outcomes if the decision threshold is not calibrated to business costs.

Evaluation gates — defined thresholds that must be met before deployment — operationalize the "good enough" decision. A threshold of AUC > 0.82 is objective; "the model looks good" is not. Teams without evaluation gates will deploy underperforming models because enthusiasm is not a quality signal.

Avoid evaluating on the same data used to select hyperparameters (validation set leakage). The test set must be held out completely until the final evaluation decision — it is a one-time use resource.

Offline evaluation measures how well the model works on historical test data. The gap between that score and real-world performance is where most production surprises hide — the test data and the live data are never perfectly the same.

cards.title: Deployment — Getting the Model into a Serving System
cards.teaser: Training produces weights; deployment produces predictions for users. The gap between them involves serialization, serving infrastructure, latency requirements, and release strategy — none of which are ML problems, but all of which determine whether ML value reaches production.

runs.text: A model that has passed evaluation must be packaged, shipped, and integrated into a system that can serve predictions at scale. Deployment is a software engineering problem with ML-specific constraints.
Deployment patterns, ordered from simplest to most operationally mature:

items.text: Batch scoring.

Run the model overnight on a dataset, write scores to a table. No latency requirement. Suitable for use cases where predictions are consumed hours or days later (credit scoring batch runs, weekly recommendation refreshes).
REST API serving.

Wrap the model in a web service (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, BentoML, Triton). Callers make synchronous HTTP requests; responses arrive in milliseconds to seconds. The dominant pattern for interactive applications.
Streaming inference.
Score events as they arrive on a message queue (Kafka, Kinesis). Suitable for real-time personalization, fraud detection, and anomaly alerting.
Edge deployment.

Export the model in a hardware-optimized format (TFLite, ONNX, CoreML) and run it on the device. Eliminates network latency and preserves privacy; trades serving infrastructure for device compatibility complexity.

runs.text: Release strategy for model deployment mirrors software: shadow deployment (run new model in parallel, log predictions, compare to champion without routing user traffic), canary (route 5% of traffic, compare metrics), blue/green (keep old version hot, switch all traffic, roll back instantly if metrics regress). The choice is driven by the cost of a bad model prediction versus the cost of delayed adoption.

Deployment is the bridge between a trained model and users getting predictions. It covers serialization, serving infrastructure, latency, and rollout strategy — all software engineering, but shaped by the fact that models can be wrong in subtle, gradual ways.

cards.title: Monitoring — Drift, Performance Decay, and System Health
cards.teaser: A deployed model is not done — it is a hypothesis about the world that needs continuous verification. Monitoring asks three questions: is the service healthy, is the input data still what we trained on, and is the model still making good predictions?

runs.text: ML monitoring combines traditional system observability with ML-specific signal. A complete monitoring setup tracks three layers:

items.text: System health.
Latency, error rate, throughput, memory usage. Standard SRE metrics. If the serving endpoint is returning 500s, none of the ML metrics matter yet.
Data drift (input drift).

The statistical distribution of features sent to the model at inference time is shifting away from the training distribution. Detected by comparing live feature statistics to a reference (training data statistics). Tools: Evidently AI, Arize, WhyLogs, Seldon Alibi Detect.
Concept drift (label drift / model performance decay).

The relationship between features and the target variable is changing. The model's predictions are becoming less accurate. Requires ground truth labels — which may arrive with latency or may not arrive at all for some use cases.

runs.text: Types of drift:

items.text: Covariate shift
— input distribution P(X) changes but P(Y|X) stays the same. The model may still work if it generalizes. Detected by input feature monitoring.
Concept drift
— P(Y|X) changes. The world's relationship between inputs and outputs has changed. The model is structurally wrong and must be retrained.
Label drift
— the output distribution P(Y) shifts. Common in fraud detection when attackers adapt to a deployed model.

runs.text: When ground truth labels are unavailable (the label arrives days later, or never), proxy metrics — prediction confidence distribution, output value distribution, business KPIs — are used as leading indicators of model degradation. A sudden increase in low-confidence predictions often precedes measurable performance decay.

Monitoring asks three questions continuously: is the system up, are the inputs still what we expected, and are the predictions still good? All three can be fine while the third is quietly failing — which is why you need all three.

cards.title: Retraining — Scheduled vs Triggered
cards.teaser: Retraining is not a sign of failure — it is the mechanism by which a model stays relevant. The design question is whether to retrain on a fixed schedule or in response to detected signal. The answer depends on drift velocity and labeling latency.

runs.text: When monitoring detects drift or performance decay, the lifecycle loops back to data collection and training. Retraining strategy is a core MLOps design decision with two primary approaches:

items.text: Scheduled retraining.

Retrain on a fixed cadence — daily, weekly, monthly — regardless of whether drift is detected. Simple to operate, predictable cost, does not require a drift detection system. Appropriate when the data distribution changes at a known, regular rate (e.g., a news recommendation model where recency matters daily).
Triggered retraining.

Retrain when monitoring signals pass a threshold: input drift exceeds a KL-divergence bound, model accuracy on a rolling window drops below a target, or a business KPI (click-through rate, conversion rate) falls outside a confidence interval. More computationally efficient than scheduled retraining, but requires a reliable monitoring and alerting stack.

runs.text: Retraining does not always help — and can hurt. Three failure modes to guard against:

items.text: Training on corrupted data.
If the upstream data pipeline has a bug that produces bad labels, retraining propagates the corruption into the new model. Data validation must gate retraining, not just the initial training run.
Feedback loop amplification.

If the model's predictions influence the data it will be retrained on (e.g., a content recommendation model whose clicks become training labels), retraining on its own predictions creates a feedback loop that narrows diversity and amplifies existing biases.
Catastrophic forgetting.

In some architectures, retraining on only recent data degrades performance on edge cases well-represented in older data. Curriculum design and training data mixing ratios must be managed deliberately.

runs.text: Retraining keeps a model current with the changing world. You can schedule it on a clock or trigger it when monitoring detects that performance has dropped. Both approaches work; triggered retraining is more efficient but requires a working monitoring stack first.

cards.title: CI, CT, and CD — Three Automation Disciplines
cards.teaser: Software pipelines have CI and CD. ML adds a third: Continuous Training. Each discipline targets a different artifact — code correctness, model freshness, and deployment safety — and all three must work together for a mature ML system.

runs.text: Google's MLOps whitepaper introduces a clean three-way distinction that is the foundation for automation design in ML systems:

items.text: Continuous Integration (CI)

— test and validate code and components. In ML, this means unit tests for feature engineering functions, integration tests for the training pipeline, and data validation tests. A code change that breaks the feature pipeline should fail CI before any training runs.
Continuous Training (CT)

— automatically retrain and evaluate the model on new data. This is the ML-unique discipline. A CT pipeline runs on a schedule or on data trigger, trains the model, runs evaluation, and promotes the model to the model registry if it passes validation gates. No human is required to initiate training.
Continuous Delivery (CD)

— automatically deploy the validated model to a serving environment. A model that passes CT gates is automatically deployed to staging; with sufficient confidence, promoted to production. Mirrors software CD, but the artifact is model weights, not a container image.

explanation.code:
Code change --> [CI] --> Tests pass --> (triggers)
Data arrival --> [CT] --> Model trained + evaluated --> Model passes gates --> (triggers)
                                                                              [CD] --> Model deployed to staging --> promoted to production

runs.text: The three disciplines are triggered by different events: CI by a code commit, CT by new data or a schedule, CD by a model passing evaluation. An organization can have strong CI but no CT — the model is retrained manually. An organization with CT but no CD pushes models to production manually. Full MLOps automation requires all three.

CI checks the code, CT automatically retrains the model when new data arrives, and CD automatically deploys the model when it passes evaluation. CI/CT/CD together mean the whole loop — code to model to production — runs without manual intervention.

cards.title: Google's MLOps Maturity Levels
cards.teaser: Google's MLOps guide defines three maturity levels — 0, 1, and 2 — that map the journey from manual, notebook-driven ML to a fully automated CI/CT/CD pipeline. Most teams operate at Level 0 and aspire to Level 1 before Level 2 becomes relevant.

runs.text: Google's "MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning" whitepaper provides the canonical maturity framework for ML operations. It defines three levels:

items.text: Level 0 — Manual process.

Data scientists train models in notebooks or scripts. Training is ad hoc, infrequent, and manually executed. The model is deployed as a prediction service with a manual, script-driven release. No pipeline, no experiment tracking, no automated retraining. The disconnect between ML and operations is large. Most real-world ML is here.
Level 1 — ML pipeline automation.

Training is automated in an ML pipeline (Kubeflow Pipelines, Vertex AI Pipelines, SageMaker Pipelines, Metaflow). The pipeline can be triggered on a schedule or on new data. Experiment tracking, data validation, and model validation are built into the pipeline. The resulting trained model is pushed to a model registry automatically. Continuous Training is achieved. The pipeline code itself is still deployed manually when changed.
Level 2 — CI/CD for ML.

The training pipeline itself is a software artifact deployed via a CI/CD system. A change to the training code triggers automated testing, pipeline deployment, and model retraining. New data triggers CT. A validated model triggers CD. The full loop is automated end to end. Teams at this level can release multiple model updates per day without manual intervention.

runs.text: The levels are not a scoring system — they are a sequencing guide. A team that skips Level 1 (pipeline automation) to attempt Level 2 (CI/CD for ML) typically fails because they are automating a process that does not yet exist in code form. The path is sequential.

Google notes that not every team needs Level 2. If the model only needs retraining quarterly and the team has one data scientist, the overhead of full CI/CD for ML is not justified. Level 1 — automated pipeline, experiment tracking, model registry — is the practical target for most teams.

Level 0 is humans running notebooks. Level 1 is an automated training pipeline that runs on new data. Level 2 is CI/CD applied to the pipeline itself, so changing the training code also deploys and retests it automatically.

cards.title: The Data-Code-Model Triple
cards.teaser: Software version control tracks one artifact: code. ML systems must version three: code, data, and model weights. Reproducibility — the ability to recreate any past model — requires all three to be linked, immutable, and retrievable.

runs.text: In software engineering, a git commit hash uniquely identifies a reproducible state of the system. In ML, three artifacts must be versioned and linked together to achieve the same reproducibility guarantee:

items.text: Code.
Training pipeline code, feature engineering, model architecture, hyperparameter configuration. Versioned in git. The training code version is a required field in any experiment record.
Data.

The specific snapshot of training data used. Versioned using DVC (Data Version Control), Delta Lake table versions, feature store snapshot IDs, or S3 object versioning. A dataset is not a filename — it is a content-addressed snapshot.
Model.

Serialized weights and model artifacts. Stored in a model registry (MLflow Model Registry, Vertex AI Model Registry, SageMaker Model Registry) with a unique version identifier, lineage back to the training run, and metadata including evaluation metrics.

runs.text: The triple is linked by the training run record: a run ID that captures the code version (git SHA), the data version (dataset snapshot ID), the hyperparameters, and the output model version. This record is what makes it possible to answer: "what produced this model, can we reproduce it, and can we compare it to the current champion?"

Organizations that version only code (common) face a specific failure mode: a model that was the best performer six months ago cannot be reproduced because the data it was trained on is no longer available in the form used. The model is a dead end — it can be served but not retrained or improved from that state.

A model in production with no versioned data lineage is an operational liability. When it needs to be retrained — and it will — the starting point cannot be recovered. The cost is a full data archaeology project or starting from scratch.

To reproduce a model you need three things: the code that trained it, the data it was trained on, and the saved weights. Version all three and link them together in a training run record, or you will lose the ability to understand or recreate past results.

cards.title: Feedback Loops — When Model Outputs Become Training Data
cards.teaser: Many production ML systems are not passive — their outputs influence user behavior, which influences the data collected, which influences the next model. These feedback loops can amplify performance or entrench errors, and failing to account for them is one of the most common sources of production ML failures.

runs.text: A feedback loop in ML occurs when model outputs are causally connected to the inputs the model will be trained on in the future. This is the rule in deployed systems, not the exception:

items.text: Recommendation systems.

The model recommends items; users click on recommended items; click data is collected as positive training signal. The model learns to recommend items that it already recommends — a popularity filter that reduces diversity over time.
Fraud detection.

The model blocks transactions it classifies as fraudulent. Future training data contains only transactions that were not blocked — the model never sees the fraud patterns it successfully stopped, causing them to fade from its learned representation.
Demand forecasting.

The model forecasts demand; procurement decisions are made based on the forecast; actual sales are influenced by procurement (stock-outs, excess inventory) — which then become the ground truth the next model is trained on.

runs.text: Feedback loops can be positive (self-reinforcing) or negative (self-correcting). Left unmanaged, positive feedback loops tend toward degenerate states: a content recommendation model that converges to recommending only viral content, a loan approval model that never approves any applicant group it has historically denied.

Mitigations include: exploration strategies (epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling) to collect off-policy signal, counterfactual logging (record what the model would have predicted for items it did not show), and offline evaluation on distributions that correct for selection bias.

A feedback loop means the model's predictions change the data the next model trains on. Recommendation systems are the clearest example: the model surfaces item A, users click on A, A gets more training signal, the model surfaces A even more. You end up training on a distorted picture of user preferences.

cards.title: The Lifecycle Varies by Model Type
cards.teaser: The six-stage loop applies to all ML — but the mechanics of each stage differ dramatically between supervised classification, unsupervised clustering, reinforcement learning, and LLM fine-tuning. Applying the wrong lifecycle pattern to the wrong model type is a common source of unnecessary MLOps complexity.

runs.text: The lifecycle structure — collect, validate, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor — is universal. The implementation of each stage is model-type-specific. Four model types illustrate the range:

items.text: Supervised learning (classification, regression).

The reference case. Labeled data is the primary cost. Evaluation is straightforward (holdout set, standard metrics). Monitoring for input drift and label drift. Retraining on new labeled data. Most MLOps tooling assumes this model type.
Unsupervised learning (clustering, anomaly detection, embeddings).

No labels required in training, but evaluation is harder — cluster quality metrics (silhouette score, Davies-Bouldin index) do not directly proxy business value. Monitoring is primarily input drift and structural change detection. "Retraining" may mean recomputing cluster centroids or re-indexing an embedding space.
Reinforcement learning.

Training generates its own data through environment interaction — the data collection and training stages are tightly coupled. Evaluation requires either live experiments (online evaluation) or high-fidelity simulation. The feedback loop is intrinsic to the algorithm. Deployment is complex: the policy must be safe to explore in a live environment.
LLM fine-tuning.

Starts from a pre-trained base model (a fundamentally different data lineage problem — you do not version ImageNet, you version your fine-tuning dataset). Evaluation requires human raters or LLM-as-judge for open-ended tasks. Monitoring for output quality is harder than monitoring for distributional drift. Safety evaluation (red-teaming, refusal rate) is a lifecycle stage with no supervised-learning equivalent.

runs.text: The practical implication: when adopting an MLOps platform or designing a lifecycle, identify the dominant model type in your system first. A platform designed for supervised classification (most of them) will require significant extension or workaround for RL or LLM fine-tuning use cases.

The lifecycle loop is the same for all model types, but each stage looks different depending on whether you are doing supervised classification, unsupervised clustering, reinforcement learning, or fine-tuning a large language model. Match your MLOps tooling to the model type you actually have.
